review:
[h1][b]My score: 7.5/10[/b][/h1]
Playthrough time: 16 hours 30 min (single player: main story and most side quests, listening to most conversation)

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
+Good action RPG combat, severing orc limbs is fun
+Lots of well put together LotR story elements/locations for fans to enjoy
+Enough levelling and loot to keep things interesting

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
-Gameplay can probably get repetitive if you play more than 1-2 hours each time
-Combat system and leveling/skill tree isn't that deep for hardcore players
-Fiddly character change system
-A few glitches may crash the game

[h1]Performance notes:[/h1]
The game is great for using the Xbox 360 controller and playing on the TV from the couch.
Graphics performance R9 280X, 1080P max settings: 60 FPS (V-sync) all the time except for a few stutters when loading new textures.

[h1]Main review:[/h1]
If you will enjoy LotR: War in the North depends on how you're going to play the game, and if you're a fan of the LotR world. The game is best played casually a few hours at the time, If you play it that way, and you're a fan, the game will probably keep you entertained all the way through and has a lot going for it when it comes to the story and locations.

If you're not interested in the Lord of the Rings world, and come just for the action RPG, you'll probably find the game lacking, especially if you put 3-4 or more hours in to the game each go, then the game will probably feel quite repetitive.

The game tells a story of three heroes (man, dwarf, elf) indirectly helping the fellowship during the LotR story. You run in to quite a few characters from the books/movies, and visit familiar locations as Bree and Rivendell. The locations in this game generally look great, and all the characters has quite a lot to say, so the story builds up well with lots of background information available if you like to listen to conversation.

The main part of the game has you battling mostly orcs in a third person action RPG style. The combat style doesn't differ much through the game, you can select any of the three characters (but switching between them is only allowed upon clearing a section of the current chapter, or after visiting towns, and is a bit clunky), use a light or heavy attack, ranged attacks and magic/skills. You level up and unlock/improve skills and get better gear/other loot that improve stats, but the gameplay doesn't change that much. You're still hacking/shooting at orcs most of the time.

I really enjoyed the combat, and the levelling/loot was enough to keep me interested all the way through, and combat is fun. Sometimes after getting the enemy HP down enough you get a prompt to use a heavy attack for a limb severing finish that for me never got old. Just as satisfying every time.

The game has some nice boss battles as well, and every chapter has a few events that mixes things up. 

The game also supports online co op (up to 3 players in total). Unfortunately, I haven't been able to try this, but I can image this game can be lots of fun with 1-2 friends.

As for the glitches: At the final chapter, there was a game breaking glitch, for some reason when navigating the tunnels the game got really choppy and crashed when the frame rate got too low. Apparently a common problem, and the solution was to set the graphics to minimum and get through that section with as little on screen as possible (aiming at the floor while moving helped). When out of the tunnels, restart the game and everything is well again.

Lord of the Rings: War in the North surprised me. I bought it expecting that it wouldn't be very good, as movie adaptations often suffer from a multitude of issues. This one, though it does have some issues, manages to avoid the worst of them.

It does so by not making the main story or characters have anything to do with the content of the movies, instead focusing on some other folks doing a different quest during the same time span. You get to cross paths with the heroes of the main story, but your story does not really impact the main events of the movies. Some have criticized the game for this, but if you look at it as just another adventure in the lands of MIddle Earth, it's fine.

War in the North takes you through a series of events unfolding, unsurprisingly, in the north part of Tolkien's maps. The villain is a bit contrived, but the rest of the journey is filled with the same kind of delicious aesthetic that the movies used to bring Middle Earth to life. I don't remember everything in the appendices of the novels, so I don't know how much of this stuff they just made up for the game, but it's all believably Tolkienesque enough that you won't think about it much unless you're a Tolkien scholar. In short, they nailed the flavour perfectly.

The gameplay is solid third-person action-RPG fare. Controls and movements are fluid, there are skill trees, and item upgrades galore. Each of the three characters plays differently enough, while still allowing the player to customize the skills and abilities toward their preferences. All characters are capable at both melee and ranged combat, all have damage-boosting abilities, and all have support abilities, so you get to decide what you want to be good at.

There are a couple issues I found with the game, namely the crafting system feels tacked-on and falls short of its potential. Inventory space is limited as well, so you run out of room for all the crafting materials. The two issues are certainly related. Part of that stems from the fact that you occasionally get gems that you can socket in your items, but using them means that you must either destroy them or the item you put them in, which disincentivizes their use. Further, they're rare to find, and have randomly generated stats, like all the rest of the gear. Which is another sore spot.

Gear. The game tries to do the fun loot hunt minigame, but falls short. The items generate very random stats. It incentivizes collecting "set" items that unlock powerful additional bonuses, but there are so many of them and not enough drops happening to make that worthwhile. I found that I was better off just using the best individual pieces of gear, regardless of set.

Sidequests are all pretty bland, fetch-quest type stuff, and kind of feel like filler, or an excuse to involve a given character in the story. Not a high-point, but could be worse.

Each area has enough secrets in it to keep you going back for more if exploration is your thing, and you will have to go through with each of the 3 characters (or play multiplayer coop) in order to find them all. That's not a bad thing necessarily, as I found the world was a joy to explore for the mostpart, and each of the characters was fun to use and level up.

Lord of the Rings: War in the North" is one of those PRECIOUS few titles  that provides satisfying, Tolkien-lore combat in a linear-style RPG progression format.
Play as the roguish Dunedain Ranger, the mighty dwarf warrior, or the magic-casting she-elf. Take on the swarming troops and big brutes of Mordor directly as your quest shapes you and your companions into a small but powerful force capable of leading the bulk of Sauron's forces away from Frodo and the rest of The Fellowship of The Ring. Meet nearly every character depicted in the movies at some point.
Combat's pretty straightforward: the pointy end goes in the bad guys. Hack and slash with a few ranged abilities and special abilities for each character to upgrade when you level up. This does allow you to specialize your character a bit more, choosing to plunk more points into ranged attacks over higher health, or better damage output with swords instead of expertise with shields. This is crucial as you progress with a buddy and balance your combat styles. If you like to mostly stay put and cut your enemies down only when they get close enough, your friend can play the sniper with arrows or ranged magic attacks. Build "aggression" by successfully attacking your foes, which makes you more likely to draw attacks from enemies, but also fuels your power attacks.
You can customize the appearance of your character, both by choosing some presets for faces and hairstyles, and by equipping different armors/armor pieces (with different armor values and specific bonuses).
The CONS: nothing major, but the shouts from each character get quite repetitive. The dwarf in particular tends to get somewhat irritating because he yells all. the. time.
Also, the game suffers a bit just from trying to reproduce the voices of actors like Sir Ian McKellen, Hugo Weaving, and Viggo Mortensen. It's not altogether bad, but for hardcore movie fans, it's probably distracting ("That doesn't sound like Aragorn at all!"). If you require sophisticated plot twists and subtleties in character to immerse yourself in a video game's story line, you probably won't get much out of LOTR: WITN. At its heart, it's a good excuse to fight orcs and Uruk-hai, and it doesn't aim much higher. If you're cool with that, then LET'S HUNT SOME ORC!

[h1]The Lord of the Rings: The War in the North[/h1]
[i]One ring to co-op them all[/i]

[i]The Lord of the Rings: War in the North[/i] is one of those games that never made massive headlines upon release despite the insane popularity of the source material and the films by Peter Jackson and was considered by all intents and purposes a flop, yet somehow this game has quietly carved out a loyal fan base thanks to its satisfying combat, gritty tone, and cooperative focus. While not without flaws and is definitely a product of its time, it delivers a surprisingly engaging action-RPG experience that respects Tolkien’s world while expanding its lesser-explored corners.

[u][b]Strengths[/b][/u]

[i][b]A darker, grittier Middle-earth[/b][/i]
Unlike most Lords of the Rings games, [i]War in the North[/i] doesn’t retread the journey of the Fellowship. Instead, it explores what was happening behind the scenes—your party battling Sauron’s northern forces while Aragorn and company handle the main quest. This gives the game freedom to introduce new characters, locations, and lore while staying true to Tolkien’s atmosphere.

[i][b]Satisfying hack-and-slash combat[/b][/i]
Combat feels weighty and visceral, although it does lack the more modern controls of the action RPG of being able to lock onto enemies or target between enemies. The three playable characters—Eradan the Ranger, Andriel the Elf mage, and Farin the Dwarf warrior—offer distinct playstyles that make co-op genuinely fun. Executing brutal slow-motion finishing moves is a lot of fun to watch when you manage to pull them off, and the loot-driven progression loop scratches the action-RPG itch nicely.

[i][b]Great co-op[/b][/i]
This is arguably the best way to play the game. With friends, the synergy between classes shines, and battles feel bigger and more tactical. Solo play is fine, but co-op elevates the entire experience and this is the route I would encourage most players to take.

[i][b]Faithful Lords of the Rings atmosphere[/b][/i]
The score, the art direction, and even some returning voice actors give the game a strong sense of authenticity when compared to the trilogy of films. Fans of Middle-earth will find a lot to love here, and that is even coming from someone who isn't the biggest The Lord of the Rings fan.

[u][b]Weaknesses[/b][/u]

[i][b]Rough edges and dated design[/b][/i]
Even at release the game had uneven polish, and today the animations, enemy AI, and visuals feel dated. Occasional bugs and odd difficulty spikes can disrupt the experience.

[i][b]A story that’s serviceable but not memorable[/b][/i]
While the premise is cool, the narrative rarely reaches the emotional or cinematic heights seen in other Lord of the Ring games or RPG's in general. Characters are likeable but not deeply developed and come across as quite bland.

[i][b]Repetition sets in[/b][/i]
Enemy variety and mission structure can become predictable. The fun, but sometimes clunky combat carries the game, but by the final act you may feel like you’re repeating the same encounter formulas where the game likes to throw wave upon wave of ever increasingly difficult and bullet-spongy enemies your way.

[i][b]Conclusion[/b][/i]

[i]The Lord of the Rings: War in the North[/i] is a rough but flawed gem, that is full of heart and clearly respects the source material its adapting from. Its combat, co-op focus, and faithful Middle-earth tone make it a great Lord of the Rings title, even if its repetitive design keep it from being an all out co-op classic. For fans of action-RPGs or Tolkien’s world, it’s absolutely worth playing.

Let me preface this review by saying [i]do [b]NOT[/b] play this game by yourself.[/i] It's really boring and frustrating as the AI for your companions can be a little stupid.

Summary:

If you're looking for a good co-op experience, this game really brings back the old Lord of the Rings: Return of the King gameplay with some nice surprises like loot for your character and while it's not very appealing to the eyes and the story is silly, the experience you get from the co-op gameplay outweighs all that.

Things I like about this game:
[list]
[*]RAndomized Loot (Players will not find hte same loot in chests and stashes and there are even item sets that you can complete)
[*]Leveling up is similar to borderlands, There are three branches of the skill tree, each focusing on a specific aspect of your character's class
[*]Up to 3 player Co-Op (LAN or Internet connection)
[*]Encourages and rewards exploration of levels (even though the game is linear, there are secret stashes of loot that players can find if they take a little extra time to explore the level)
[*]Small Mini Quests
[*]Orcs and Goblins are the main enemy here but there are also other enemies like Undead that you face as well
[/list]
Things I don't like about this game
[list]
[*]The animation of the bad guys seems like it was worked on more than the good guys, and the good guys animation feels stiff
[*]I think even by 2011's standards the graphics are a little lack-luster
[*]The beginning is bassically "3 heros meet in a bar and talk to Aragorn and decide to go slay some Orcs, have at it player" there's not a strong sense of direction here as to what you need to do when you first start your new game

[h1]The Lord of the Rings: The War in the North: for late arrivals[/h1]

I was first introduced to The War in the North by my brother in 2013. He had picked up the game looking for a co-op campaign to play with some friends. I am a fan of LOTR and a co-op RPG looked fun. I watched my brother play through the game as the Human Ranger.

As a result the following has been spoiled:
[list]
[*]The plot was spoiled
[*]The missions were spoiled
[*]The combat was spoiled
[*]The location of secrets were spoiled
[/list]
In February 2018, I decided to pickup and play the game with my brother and another friend as the Elf Mage.

I expected The War in the North to be a quick hack and slash campaign that was overall an average experience.

[i]Is it worth your time? Even if everything is spoiled?[/i]

[b]-Yes but only if you have friends to play with (who do not have AMD graphics cards)-[/b]

I am going to get the problems out of the way first.
[list]
[*]AMD users will experience random crashes and loss of EXP progress during these crashes. There are fixes in the Steam forums but we just powered through it. 
[*]The lobby will also drop at random times and must be remade. Checkpoints are frequent so progression is not significantly hindered. 
[*]The game will force ingame voice chat which sounds horrible and we used a virtual audio cable to work around this. 
[*]BOT AI is not very good and defense missions will be unreasonably difficult in singleplayer. 
[/list]
If you are not willing to work around these problems [b]DO NOT[/b] buy The War in the North. 
 
Now for the reasons why I recommend it anyway.

The melee combat is extremely simple (light attack until a yellow triangle appears, then heavy attack) but the spells and abilities of the main trio are really fun to use. As the Elf Mage, I started the game as a healer/support caster but later unlocked abilities that turned me into a super tank. 

The missions and story were straight forward but the levels were well paced. There is plenty of loot to find and traders are placed throughout the mission to empty your generously sized inventory. The voice acting by all of the NPCs were likely better than the main trio.

Three player co-op is the best experience because all of your abilities synergize really well. After a few missions, you will be saving, healing, and buffing your teammates like a natural. If it wasn't for the crashes, I could see myself replaying the game with different characters or on a harder difficulty.

[b]Play The War in the North with friends because it is worth the effort. Where else are you going to destroy hordes of enemies as a discount version of The Three Hunters?[/b]

[h3]The Lord of the Rings: War in the North[/h3]

A really interesting made Action-Adventure in the Lord of the Rings Franchise. Leaning near the Storyline of the Books, the Player will travel with another Group of Heroes to fight against one of Sauron’s Henchmens to stop him from invading the north of Middle-earth.

You take control of one of 3 heroes and follow their journey through various in the Books mentioned places either alone or with up to 2 friends in Coop while fighting off hords of Goblins, Orcs and other hostile Forces.
And finishing some Peoples tasks if you accept their Quest to get rewarded with helpful Items to equip your Character and become even more powerful in the combats to come.

The Games strength is in the nice delivery of a Middle-Earth themed Environment to the Player and the oportunity to fight hords of Orcs and other Monsters.
Also the freedom of the Skilltree is well made and gives a lot of Options for individuality.
And besides of the Gameplay it also implemented nice sections to give more Information of the world of middle-earth for those who want to know more about the Lord of the Rings Franchise.

Still there has also be to mentioned the negatives too. And so the Games sadly fails a little when it comes to the combat Mechanics themself, often the Characters not exactly doing what they should do, or targeting different enemies then the one directly close to the player, or getting hit while in dodge animation.
Also the extra Maps (Arenas) where extremly unbalanced and gave a weird level recommendation compaired to the more poiwerfull enemies it spawned during higher waves.

How i would like to recommend this Game to People, but sadly it is no longer available to get purchased.
So if you are a Lord of the Ring Fans and like Action-Adventure Games and somehow be able to come across a still working Edition (License) then i would say this game could be one to enjoy for you.

GAMEPLAY: Basic hack-and-slash action game, very little tactics. The skills you acquire throughout the game are handy in later levels, but offer very little variety and leveling, this game can therefore hardly be called an RPG. Enemies are often copy-pasted from earlier-chapter variations and offer little in terms of tactical variety. The bosses are sometimes tough, but more often than not easy. The most unfortunate thing was the last boss in the game, who was extremely easy to beat. The stores and interfaces are clunky, and often do not work as you would want them to, even crashing or having to re-open sometimes.

STORY: From a video game/fantasy perspective, the story is average. From a Tolkien-reader perspective, the story is horrible. Orcs and humans who use dark magic, goblins who blow themselves up with bombs, an entire never-heard-of timeline? J.R.R. Tolkien would turn in his grave if he had ever seen this game, and I can imagine heir Christopher isn't too happy with this either. A typical example of licensing gone wrong. Had this been a generic fantasy game in another setting, I would have judged the story as average but fun, but since this is misuse of the "Lord of the Rings" name, I have to be angry with it.

BUGS AND FLAWS: I played through this game via online multiplayer with my younger brother (we live in different cities). He has a medium gaming PC that plays most of the newest games at good settings, yet during a few levels, notably chapters 2 and 8, he experienced severe lag. At first we thought it was our online connection, but it turned out this is a well-known flaw that many players experience during this game, especially with ATI/AMD graphics cards. Secondly, if you join the game of a player that is farther ahead than you, you cannot save or gain achievements. One time, my brothers game crashed at an inopportune moment (chapter 2, right during the cutscene before the boss), while mine saved when the boss battle started. I quit, but alas, we had to retry everything. When he tried to get to the same point in a solo game, it turned out his save was corrupted and the game wouldn't load the boss into his arena. Therefore, we started the ENTIRE game again from the beginning. This time, when we got to the final boss battle in chapter 8, the boss wouldn't load into the arena. After the second time rebooting the game and reloading this save, he finally loaded and we could finish the game. By this time, my heart was already pounding, fearing we would have played through the entire game and not be able to finish the last battle.

In all, if you don't care about the most beautiful of worlds that J.R.R. Tolkien has created, if you don't care about variety in gameplay, and if you don't care about repetitiveness and some easy bosses, you can play this game for a bit of fun. But please, PLEASE play it on another platform. Unless you also don't care about major crashes, corrupted saves and restarting from scratch halfway through a game, of course... ;)

Please don't confuse this game with the turn-based RPG, "The Lord of the Rings: The Third Age" that was released in 2004. They are very different games with very similar narrative structures. This is a third-person action RPG in the style of a dungeon crawler.

This game isn't really anything special. It's a lot like the original Baldur's Gate (the console dungeon crawler version, not the PC RPG) in that there are three characters to play, each with their own strengths and specialties, upgradable armor and weapons, and hack-and-slash style gameplay. The only thing that sets it apart is that it has the "Lord of the Rings" license (the Peter Jackson movies, specifically), and although it uses characters from that franchise their likenesses and voices are a bit spotty. 

You don't actually play as any of the characters from the books or movies, as this is a side-story style game set during the events of those adventures. You take control of either the ranger Eradan, the elven sorceress Andriel, or the dwarven lore-master Farin, and whichever two characters you don't pick are controlled by the game's AI. Your quarry is the evil sorcerer Agandaur, the so-called "Right Hand of Sauron" as he tries to put some schemes into place that will help the Dark Lord conquer all of Middle Earth. Like I said, it's not exactly original or anything, but it is implemented fairly well.

As this game has RPG elements, you'll find your self getting the same experience points, levelling up the same stats, and climbing the same skill trees that you've seen in a hundred games before and since, but it's all functional and works well here. So far, I think this game got a bad rap. LOTR: War in the North is a fairly straight forward action based rpg, which nevertheless brings on many hours of fun.

Plot: the game seeks to expand on Tolkien's Middle Earth by presenting a side story that happens along side the War of the Rings. You get to play as either Eradan the ranger, Andriel the lore-master, or Farin the champion, to thwat the plans of Sauron's commander, Agandaur. While exploring vast landscape from the Shire, to Grey Mountains, and Mirkwood, you get to meet members from the fellowship of the rings, side characters such as Radagast the Brown, and even a mighty dragon. If you've played LOTR: the Third Age, the narrative of this game is fairly similiar.

Gameplay: the 3 aspects of a good RPG are present in this game, namely - statpoints, skilltree, and itemization. As there are limited points and inventory space to go around, decisions must be made into how your character is created. While the diversity of types of character is definitely limited, it is enough to keep you entertained for a 20-50hrs long game.

Unlike The Third Age, this game is a action based RPG and each 'encounter' with orcs requires some sort of finesse to defeat them. However, the game is not too hard, and it actually becomes easier as you unlock the heroic, and legendary difficulty levels. On the same note, a major flaw in this game is that the difficulty is based on the character you choose *winks* Farin, rather than the level you are playing on. Also, unlocking the 'legendary' difficutly, requires you to complete the game two times on it's fairly short storyline. This may get boring, although the lure of better items, hitting the maximum level, and uncovering all the secrets/collecting all 50 achievements is enough to keep a player going. 

Quests in this game is fairly one dimensional as most of them cannot be missed as long as you diligently explore the maps and talk to the NPCs. More details shoud be added to the  backstory to make this game more vibrant and interesting. 'Secrets' on the other hand requires some time spent exploring and manipulation of the ever annoying 'game save' mechanics, and this may frustrate players unless they find a guide (which there are surprisingly few online). 

Lastly, this game UI is clearly based on the console version, and some mechanics such as character movement and inventory management, feels clunky and poorly done up. However, this is not a problem after taking some time getting used to it, although, a PC game controller will certainly improve the experience.

Audio/visual: the landscapes and character design are extremely well done for a 2011 game with details such as seeing the weaves in Elrond's shirt, rock patterns in the background, and blood splatter as you chop off the orc's head. While the game's background music and action sounds are vibrant, the voice acting could be better, to add more life to the storyline, and make the hero jouney seems more epic. Together, the atmosphere of the game felt a letdown as the good visuals such as the never ending rain in Bree is not complimented with audio effects to bring about an immersive expierence.

Verdict: Overall, War in the North gets more fun as you progress along the difficulty levels, and your character feels truely powerful on the final difficulty level. However, the clunky mechanics, limited depth to the character's development, quests and backstory limits this game from  being an epic RPG. Also the game design restrict it to around 60hrs of gameplay before it gets repetitive. Thus, this game would be a good buy during steam sales as a form of pasttime, but definitely not a must-have, unless you are a Lord of the Rings fan.

Disclaimer: this review is written based on solo-play only, and I have yet to encounter any bugs with this game.

Greetings, fellow gamers! Strap on your mythril helmets and pack some lembas bread because today, we're venturing into Middle-earth for the lesser-known holiday destination: the northern wastes, where "The Lord of the Rings: War in the North" unfolds. This game promises thrills, spills, and the occasional frostbite!

Graphics:
The landscapes are so pretty, you'll almost forget they're teeming with bloodthirsty orcs. Almost. The snow sparkles underfoot, which is lovely until a troll decides to make you part of the scenery. The character models are detailed enough to see the angst on every elf’s face, because what’s an elf without a little existential dread?

Gameplay:
The combat is as smooth as Gandalf’s beard is long. Swing your sword, cast your spells, and occasionally yell at your computer when your allies decide that staring at walls is more important than fighting. The co-op mode is fantastic—nothing says "team bonding" like collectively trying not to die in the frozen tundra.

Story:
It’s like someone threw the main LOTR plot into a blender, added a dash of forgotten lore, and hit "puree." You won’t find Frodo or the gang here, but you do get to befriend an eagle, which honestly, should be a feature in every game. Your quest? To ensure that the main heroes' story can happen by handling all the dirty work up North. Yes, you're basically Middle-earth's unsung janitorial staff.

Voice Acting:
Imagine hiring the most epic voice actors and then forgetting to write epic lines. Every now and then, someone delivers a line with such gravitas you'll feel compelled to salute your screen. Most times, though, you'll be giggling at the melodrama.

Replay Value:
Why play once when you can play thrice and still not understand the subplot about the dwarf’s lost recipe for stew? Each playthrough reveals new ways to accidentally get your teammates killed, which is always a plus in my book.

Co-op Mode:
The cooperative mode in 'The Lord of the Rings: War in the North' is a true gem, elevating the gameplay experience from a solitary slog to a merry melee with friends. As you and your pals navigate through frostbitten landscapes and face off against menacing foes, the game turns into a rollicking series of mishaps and heroic saves. The shared joy (and occasional frustration) of strategising, battling, and inevitably reviving each other after daring (and sometimes foolish) maneuvers, makes each session not just a fight for Middle-earth, but a party in its most perilous corners. Nothing quite beats the laughter and camaraderie of conquering a troll with friends, only to accidentally blast each other off a cliff moments later!

In conclusion, "The Lord of the Rings: War in the North" is the perfect game for those who’ve ever thought, "You know what 'The Fellowship of the Ring' needed? More snow and side quests!" Dive in for the epic battles, stay for the accidental comedy of AI companions walking into rocks. Happy gaming! 🎮

Okay, so, I spent an hour writing out a lengthy review of this filled with insight, in depth information, pros, cons, and fully described aspects of the game with no spoilers. Then Steam decided it was going to not going to let my review go through, then proceeded to crash before I could copy what I had written (lesson learned: type out the review in Word or Notepad before copying it here). 

Because I don't have the energy to write out that lengthy of a review anymore, we're going to shorten what I wrote down to the important aspects of it.

Rating 3.5/5

-0.5 points for Difficulty scaling

The game has a co-op feature for up to three people. I beat the final boss in less than five minutes on the first try, yet other battles in the game took me an hour because I was playing solo. The game shouldn't punish me for playing solo. I shouldn't need to cover two different sides of a battle with hopeless AI that can't do it for me when solo playing.

-0.5 points for Combat/Mechanics

I chose to play just the dwarf for the entirety of the game rather than switching in between missions. Perhaps sticking with one character was the wrong choice because the combat is overly repetitive. Once you unlock some of the skills, it becomes a tad more varied, but then quickly goes back to repetitiveness. Atack, attack, dodge roll, attack, skill 123, attack, rinse and repeat. Nothing special. Also, there is no jump but instead a dodge roll, which is fine. However, there are many aspects of the game where the designers definitely made it seem like there was a secret on a ledge, but lo and behold, you can't jump. A few bugs where you can't attack, or can't hit a crate, or can't move around an object were present, but didn't take away from the experience.

-0.5 points for Miscellaneous

Lack of a save function other than visiting a shop or travelling to a different place. And my biggest gripe is the inability to compare weapons when trying to buy something. I shouldn't have to look at my gear, memorize the stats, go into the shop, look at the boots there, realize I forgot the stats of my equipped item, back out, and do it all over again. That is beyond tedious. And the last miscellaneous complaint is the challenge missions. Much like any game like this, there are challenge missions where you have to defeat multiple waves of enemies. Unfortunately, after spending 30 minutes on a challenge mission, you get nothing for beating it other than the experience from killing the monsters. I went through 20 healing pots and didn't get a single reward for my troubles?

+1 point for Visuals/Voiceover 

The game isn't anything spectacular visually (it IS five years old), but it has a certain charm to it and does what it can to honor the world of Middle Earth. The voiceover work was a real great point of interest for me as a voice actor. Most of the voice over was well done with fantastic casting. 

+1 point for Lore/Story

For any fans of the books/movies, this game definitely does a good job of immersing you into familiar territory. There will be quite a few familiar faces, and a whole myriad of new ones. There are familiar locations like Rivendell and Bree, and a few new ones like Nordinbad (a Dwarven city). 

+1 point for Skills/Gear/Leveling

This one was on the fence for me. I was afraid the system was going to be too simple, but it turns out it's rather nice. Leveling up grants three points to be spent in either Strength (melee damage), Stamina (health), Will (mana), or Dexterity (ranged damage). Then you get to put one point in your skill tree. Each character has three active skills you can unlock with respective trees underneath those skills. Unfortunately, each tree has randomly thrown in skills that often don't have anything to do with the skill you unlocked. The gear isn't visually impressive. Finding a new sword won't WOW you visually, but a clear stat difference can be seen when using it in combat. I could go into more detail, but, the entire system is just meh, but I don't have many complaints on it.

Overall, the game isn't too bad. The replayability is pretty good because once you beat it on normal mode, you unlock heroic mode where you can play through again but stay the same level so you can unlock more things and get better gear. I would recommend playing it with a friend rather than going solo. 

tl;dr 

Not bad. Not good. If you're a fan of LotR, give it a try. Play with a friend.

You follow three companions (Eradan, Andriel and Farin) on their quest to defeat a minion of the dark lord Sauron. On their way they make several friends and stops in the north of Middle Earth.

[b]GRAPHICS:[/b] Not bad at all for a game that is already 4 years old. We saw a fair amount of detail on armours, buildings and the like and didn’t realise we were playing such an old game.

[b]INTERFACE:[/b] Convenient use of hotkeys and a useful minimap! The inventory was a little off, since you had very limited space and images for additional and trivial objects in the world of Middle Earth.

[b]GAMEPLAY:[/b] We found it very useful that you could see the name of your friends on screen even if they were in an entirely different place/room. A very useful feature of the game is that you have the option to exchange items with other players that are only suitable for that particular race. Conveniently enough there were several sell/buy/return to civilisation-points.

- [u]For the Ranger:[/u] Very smooth movement of the character during a fight and one of the current reviewers enjoyed the swordplay a little too much at times. We liked the convenient switch between two-handed, one-handed, dual wielding and bow very useful. And, contrary to some other RPG’s,  the realism of being attacked whilst you are looting or switching weapons was very satisfactory to us! We loved the critical, brutal, legendary, etc. strikes with the swords and headshots with the bow too. They lead to some pretty funny ways of dying! We would’ve loved an alternative attack with hotkey ‘2’ while using a two-handed sort, but that could just be because we didn’t unlock every skill in the skill tree. Conclusion; Eradan was a great ranger.
- [u]For the Lore-master:[/u] Andriel has some great abilities to use in combat, as a supportive mage. For example, she can conjure a magical shield that can protect you against arrows and magical blasts. She also can use her staff as a melee weapon, that is actually quite strong. Because of her Elven ancestry, Andriel can use herbs to fabricate potions to support herself or her companions. This can be decisive at some points in the game.
- [u]For the Champion:[/u] Not applicable (yet), but Farin is awesome!! He got us out of trouble more than once…more like a thousand times…LOL. 

[b]ALSO FUN;[/b]
	- You can use your Eagle friend to do all the heavy work for you.
	- You meet a dragon; Which seems to be very popular amongst gamers.
	- Turrets!

[b][u]Overall conclusion:[/u][/b] 'The Lord of the Rings - War in the North' is a must have if you are a fan of the LOTR, RPG and/or co-op gaming, with a bit of hack & slash in it. We had hours and hours of fun (and yet more to come) and we didn't get bored with the storyline once, even though all those trolls were a pain. Me and my friend decided that we definitely are going to play this game a few times each year... *Totally not addicted*
